doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: Soloing with Miles and being cued off
summary: Playing the 'Human Nature' feature with Miles Davis and watching for his cue to end solos.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: It all works. Where I was going was that when I listen to it and, you know how YouTube is, you’re watching something and then over on the right hand side you might want to watch this. There was this video of you playing with Miles and an extended solo, and you were like really giving it all you had and you’re surrounded by electronic instruments, and the contrast between those two pieces of music was very telling. I wondered when you were playing with Miles in that kind of situation did you ever get into a situation where you’re playing and playing and in your head you’re thinking okay Miles, I’m done now? Like can we move on?

Maybe. Yeah. Because we all had usually one solo of the night that was our main feature. I took other solos throughout the night with him but there’s that one, it’s on “Human Nature,” the Michael Jackson song. And it was just concert A minor, so B minor — are you a tenor player? I didn’t ask earlier.

So it was an A minor concert, so B minor for us, and you know I think that I mean he was so aware of what was going on that he sometimes probably let me go past that point where I thought I was finished just to force me to find something else. And I’ll tell you,

that feeling was better than feeling like I had more to go and then have him cut me off, which sometimes, occasionally that happened where I felt like I was not really finished but you know you’re kind of playing, yeah because of course you don’t tell him when you’re finished, he’s going to come and tell you. So you’re kind of playing and you get to a certain point in your solo where you know it’s about that time where it might be close to the end so kind of playing but looking over your shoulder to see where he was.
You mean physically where he was?
Yeah, because he would usually kind of come over and when he was close to you he would kind of play something that would cue the band and that was it.
